---
title: "The Twenty-Two"
subtitle: "Every position on the field, what each one actually does, and why the person wearing the jersey matters less than where he stands and what he's been told to do."
description: "The eleven offensive, eleven defensive and handful of special-teams positions, named and explained: who blocks, who carries, who can legally catch a pass, how jersey numbers tell officials (and you) who's eligible, why bodies match jobs, and the difference between a player's position, his alignment and his assignment."
glossary:
  "Quarterback": "The offensive player who takes the snap on almost every play, hands the ball off or throws it, and usually relays the play call and makes the pre-snap adjustments."
  "Running back": {def: "The offensive back whose main job is to carry the ball on running plays; he also catches short passes and blocks blitzers. Lines up behind or beside the quarterback.", aliases: ["Halfback"]}
  "Fullback": "A bigger, blocking-first back who lines up in front of or beside the running back and leads him into the hole; now a rare, specialist position in the NFL."
  "Wide receiver": "A pass-catcher who lines up away from the linemen, near the sideline (split out wide) or in between (the slot). His main job is running routes and catching passes."
  "Tight end": "A hybrid of lineman and receiver who often lines up right next to a tackle (tight to the line), blocks on running plays and runs routes on passing plays."
  "Offensive line": "The five players in the middle of the offense (center, two guards, two tackles) who block on every play and may not catch forward passes."
  "Center": "The offensive lineman in the middle of the line who snaps the ball to the quarterback and then blocks; he usually also identifies which defender the blocking scheme counts from."
  "Guard": "One of the two offensive linemen on either side of the center."
  "Tackle (position)": "One of the two offensive linemen on the outside of the line, next to the guards; usually the tallest, longest-armed linemen, whose main job is blocking pass rushers off the edge."
  "Defensive tackle": "A defensive lineman who lines up inside, across from the guards or center, to clog the middle against the run and push the pocket on passes."
  "Nose tackle": "The defensive tackle lined up on (or nearly on) the center, usually the biggest player on the defense; in a three-man line, the middle lineman."
  "Defensive end": "A defensive lineman who lines up at or near the end of the defensive line, outside the offensive tackles; his main jobs are rushing the passer and keeping runs from getting outside."
  "Edge rusher": "The modern catch-all name for the defender whose main job is pressuring the quarterback from outside the offensive tackle, whether he's called a defensive end or an outside linebacker."
  "Linebacker": "A defender who lines up behind the defensive line (the second level) and does a bit of everything: tackling runners, covering short passes and sometimes rushing the passer."
  "Mike linebacker": "The middle linebacker (M), usually the defense's signal-caller, lined up in the middle of the formation."
  "Will linebacker": "The weak-side linebacker (W), lined up on the side of the formation away from the tight end; usually the fastest linebacker, who chases plays from behind."
  "Sam linebacker": "The strong-side linebacker (S), lined up on the tight end's side of the formation; usually the biggest linebacker, often the one taken off the field for a fifth defensive back."
  "Cornerback": "A defensive back who lines up across from the wide receivers, usually near the sideline, and covers them on passing plays."
  "Slot cornerback": {def: "A cornerback who covers the slot receiver, lining up inside between the outside corner and the linemen; the fifth defensive back in a nickel defense.", aliases: ["Nickel back"]}
  "Safety (position)": "A defensive back who lines up deepest, usually 10 to 15 yards off the ball, as the last line of defense against deep passes and long runs."
  "Free safety": "The safety who usually plays deeper and more in the middle of the field, 'free' to go wherever the ball goes rather than covering a particular receiver."
  "Strong safety": "The safety who usually lines up on the strong (tight end) side, a little closer to the line, and helps more against the run."
  "Kicker": "The specialist who kicks field goals, extra points and kickoffs."
  "Punter": "The specialist who punts the ball away on fourth down, standing about 15 yards behind the line."
  "Long snapper": "The specialist who snaps the ball the long distance back to the punter or holder on kicking plays."
  "Holder": "The player, usually the punter, who catches the long snap on a field goal or extra point and sets the ball on the ground for the kicker."
  "Returner": "The player on the receiving team who catches a kickoff or punt and tries to run it back."
  "Gunner": "On a punt, one of the two players split out wide who sprint downfield to tackle the returner; the other side assigns one or two blockers (vices) to slow each of them."
  "Eligible receiver": "An offensive player allowed to catch a forward pass: one of the two players on the ends of the line, or any back (anyone lined up behind the line), except a quarterback taking the snap under center."
  "Ineligible receiver": "An offensive player who may not catch a forward pass: the interior linemen, anyone wearing 50-79 who hasn't reported as eligible, any player covered up inside the end of the line, and a quarterback taking the snap under center."
  "Skill positions": "The offense's ball-handling positions (quarterback, running back, wide receiver and tight end), as opposed to the linemen."
  "Front seven": "The defensive linemen and linebackers together, the defenders who line up near the ball and play the run first. (In a nickel defense it is often six.)"
  "Secondary": "The defensive backs as a group (cornerbacks and safeties), who line up farther from the ball and are responsible first for pass coverage."
  "Alignment": "Where a player lines up before the snap on a particular play: his spot, depth and position relative to the ball and to the other players."
  "Assignment": "A player's job on a particular play: whom he blocks, which route he runs, which gap he fills or which receiver or area he covers."

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"
import os

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, Patch, Circle
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, defense, style, show_animation, draw_marker

style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
GREEN = "#0f7a55"   # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field

# The book's marker tags (introduced in this chapter): one or two letters per position.
OFF_TAGS = {"QB": "Q", "FB": "F", "RB": "R", "Y": "Y", "U": "U", "X": "X", "Z": "Z", "H": "H",
            "LT": "LT", "LG": "LG", "C": "C", "RG": "RG", "RT": "RT"}
DEF_TAGS = {"SDE": "E", "WDE": "E", "SDT": "T", "WDT": "T", "NT": "N", "SAM": "S", "MIKE": "M",
            "WILL": "W", "LCB": "C", "RCB": "C", "NB": "$", "DB": "D", "FS": "FS", "SS": "SS"}


def tagged(players):
    """Apply the book's marker tags to a list of players."""
    out = []
    for q in players:
        table = OFF_TAGS if q.side == "off" else DEF_TAGS
        out.append(q.moved(label=table.get(q.key, q.label)))
    return out


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def P_(fld, p, d, w):
    """(d, w) in the offense's frame -> plot coordinates of this drawn field."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.6, ha="center", weight="normal"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9,
                fontweight=weight, linespacing=1.1,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.88))


def lead(fld, p, frm, to, color=style.MUTED):
    """A thin leader line from a label at `frm` to a player at `to` (both (d, w))."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P_(fld, p, *frm), P_(fld, p, *to)
    fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=0.7, zorder=7.5)


def bracket(fld, p, w, d0, d1, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7):
    """A vertical bracket at width w spanning depths d0..d1, labelled beside it."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P_(fld, p, d0, w), P_(fld, p, d1, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x0 - 0.6, x0, x1, x1 - 0.6], [y0, y0, y1, y1], color=color, lw=1.0, zorder=6)
    fld.ax.text(x0 + 0.6, (y0 + y1) / 2, text, rotation=90, fontsize=fontsize, color=color,
                ha="left", va="center", zorder=9, fontweight="bold")


def ghost(fld, p, d, w, side, label, alpha=0.5, ring=None):
    """A faded marker: where a player stands on a different snap."""
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    for a in draw_marker(fld.ax, x, y, side, label, fld.pts_per_yard()):
        a.set_alpha(alpha)
    if ring:
        fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.75 * 1.55, fc="none", ec=ring, lw=1.6, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=3.5))


def zoom_strip(p, times, lat=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-8.5, 13.5), ncols=2, width_in=6.5, labels=None):
    """A frame strip cropped to the box. (gridiron's frame_strip fits all 22 players, which makes
    run-game markers tiny.) `labels` = {time: [(d, w, text), ...]} adds a note to a panel."""
    from gridiron import draw_frame
    df = p.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"]
    ts = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(times) / ncols))
    ylo, yhi = sorted((p.ball_y - lat[0], p.ball_y - lat[1]))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / (yhi - ylo) + 0.3)))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(times):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for ax, t in zip(axes.flat, times):
        fid = int((ts - t).abs().idxmin())
        fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=p.los, window=window, lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=p.to_go,
                    numbers=False)
        cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
        inside = cur[(cur["y"] > ylo - 0.5) & (cur["y"] < yhi + 0.5) & (cur["x"] < p.los + window[1] - 0.5)]
        trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(set(inside["_id"]))]
        draw_frame(fld, inside, trails, fld.pts_per_yard())
        ax.set_title("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f}s", fontsize=9, color=style.INK_2, loc="center")
        for (d, w, text) in (labels or {}).get(t, []):
            x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
            ax.text(float(x), float(y), text, fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK, ha="center", va="center", zorder=12,
                    linespacing=1.1, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.5))
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig


# --- the chapter's two base pictures
def i_form_vs_43(te_side="right"):
    """21 personnel (I-formation: fullback and tailback stacked behind the QB) vs a base 4-3."""
    off = tagged(offense("i_form"))
    if te_side == "left":   # flip the skill players, keep the linemen's names on their own sides
        off = [q if q.key in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT") else q.mirrored() for q in off]
    off = [q.moved(label="T") if q.key == "RB" else q for q in off]
    return off, tagged(defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off))


def eleven_vs_nickel(nb_w=-8.3):
    """11 personnel from the shotgun (tight end in-line, slot receiver H on the left) vs a 4-2-5 nickel."""
    off = tagged(offense("gun_2x2"))
    off = [q.moved(d=-0.7, w=4.8) if q.key == "Y" else (q.moved(d=-1.5) if q.key == "Z" else q) for q in off]
    dfn = tagged(defense("nickel", "two_high", off, strength="right"))
    return off, [q.moved(d=5.0, w=nb_w) if q.key == "NB" else q for q in dfn]
```

Sunday, a few minutes before kickoff. The broadcast cuts to a graphic: eleven faces, each
with a name, a college and two or three letters you only half recognize. *LT. RG. FS. Sam.*
Then the game starts and the announcer is talking faster than you can follow: "The nickel
is walking down over the slot... the Mike points at the Will... the tight end is the only
one in to block..." You know the quarterback. You can probably find the running back. And the
other twenty players on the field are, for most viewers, a blur of helmets. This chapter
fixes that. By the end, every one of those twenty-two people will have a name, a job and a
reason for existing, and you'll know the one distinction that makes the rest of the book
possible: the difference between who a player *is*, where he *stands* and what he's been
told to *do*.

**You'll be able to…**

- Name all eleven offensive positions and say what each one does on a run and on a pass.
- Name the defensive positions, from the nose tackle to the free safety, and tell the Mike,
  Will and Sam linebackers apart by where the tight end lines up.
- Name the special-teams specialists (kicker, punter, long snapper, holder, returner, gunner)
  and find them on a kicking play.
- Say which offensive players may legally catch a forward pass, and use jersey numbers to
  check.
- Explain why a guard and a cornerback have such different bodies, using real combine data.
- Separate a player's position from his alignment and his assignment, and explain why good
  coaches blur all three on purpose.

## Twenty-two players, three teams

At any moment eleven players per side are on the field. Not the same eleven, though. An NFL
team is really three teams that share a roster: an **offense** for when it has the ball, a
**defense** for when the other side has it, and a **special teams** unit for kicking plays
(kickoffs, punts, field goals and extra points, which you met in
[The Game in Fifteen Minutes](01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)). A team carries 53
players on its roster, and up to 48 of them dress for a game.[^roster] Players come and go
between plays as freely as the coaches like.

It wasn't always this way, and how it changed explains why NFL bodies look the way they do.
For football's first half-century most players played the whole game, offense *and*
defense, which meant every player had to be a compromise: big enough to block, quick enough
to cover, fit enough to last sixty minutes. Substitution rules were strict, so a player who
came out often couldn't go back in that quarter. The NFL loosened them during the Second
World War, when rosters were thin, and made **unlimited free substitution** permanent in
January 1950.[^platoon] Within a few years teams were using separate offensive and defensive
units ("two platoons"), and then specialists for kicking. The last great player who refused
to come off the field was the Eagles' Chuck Bednarik, a center on offense and a linebacker
on defense, who played almost all of the 1960 championship game and ended it by tackling the
Packers' Jim Taylor on the final play.[^bednarik]

Once a player only had to do one job, he could be built for that job. That is the single
biggest reason a modern roster contains 330-pound men who can't run a fast 40 and 190-pound
men who can't block anyone: each was chosen for a narrow, demanding task. We'll measure that
with real data later in the chapter.

### The whole picture first

Here are all twenty-two at once, in a traditional alignment: an offense with two backs
behind the quarterback against a classic "base" defense (four linemen, three linebackers,
four defensive backs). You'll rarely see this exact picture on a modern Sunday (we'll see
the more common one shortly), but it's the clearest way to meet every position, because each
one is in its classic spot.

**How to read the field diagrams in this book.** The offense moves up the page. The blue
line across the field is the line of scrimmage, the imaginary line through the ball that
neither side may cross before the snap (defined fully in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)); the thick
yellow-orange line is the line to gain, ten yards ahead here. Offensive players are blue
circles, defenders are orange squares, and each wears a short tag: **Q** quarterback, **T**
or **R** the running back, **F** fullback, **X**, **Z** and **H** wide receivers, **Y** (and
sometimes **U**) tight ends, and **LT LG C RG RT** the offensive linemen from left to right
(later diagrams often leave the linemen's tags off). On defense, **E** defensive end, **T**
defensive tackle, **N** nose tackle, **S M W** the Sam, Mike and Will linebackers, **C**
cornerback, **$** the slot cornerback, **FS** and **SS** the free and strong safeties. A
colored ring marks a player to watch.

```{python}
#| label: fig-whole-picture

The tight end is on the offense's right, so that is the 'strong' side: the Sam linebacker and the strong safety line up there."
off, dfn = i_form_vs_43()
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
f = p.draw(lateral=(-21.5, 24.0), window=(-9.5, 16.0), title=False)
OC, DC = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.DEFENSE_DARK
for d, w, t, ha in [(-2.3, -15, "wide receiver (X)", "center"), (-3.1, 15, "wide receiver (Z)", "center"),
                    (-0.7, 6.0, "tight end", "left"), (-2.2, 1.3, "quarterback", "left"),

                    (-2.2, -2.2, "offensive line", "right")]:

for d, w, t, ha in [(1.0, -5.3, "defensive end", "right"), (1.0, 5.6, "defensive end", "left"),
                    (2.65, 0.8, "defensive tackles", "center"), (6.0, -3.0, "Will LB", "center"),
                    (6.0, 0.8, "Mike LB", "center"), (4.0, 7.0, "Sam LB", "left"),
                    (5.6, -15, "cornerback", "center"), (5.6, 15, "cornerback", "center"),
                    (13.6, -9, "free safety", "center"), (13.6, 9, "strong safety", "center")]:
    say(f, p, d, w, t, color=DC, ha=ha)
bracket(f, p, 18.6, 0.2, 5.4, "front seven", color=DC)
bracket(f, p, 18.6, 6.2, 13.0, "secondary", color=DC)
say(f, p, 0.75, -20.0, "line of scrimmage", fontsize=6.2, ha="left")
```
